steps.stem: Consumer researchers tested a hypothesis by means of the following experiment. Each participant received a kit for a small wooden shelf, together with an instruction booklet. Half of the participants were asked to assemble the shelf on their own; the other half watched while a member of the research team assembled it for them. All of the shelves were then wrapped in paper, and each participant was asked to state the highest price they would be willing to pay for their shelf. Which of the following hypotheses did the researchers test?
choices: People are willing to pay more for a product that they can examine closely than for a product that is hidden from view
People value an object more highly if they have built it themselves than if someone else has built it for them
The clearer the instructions that accompany a product, the higher the price that people are willing to pay for it
People value a product they chose themselves more than a product that was chosen for them
explanation: The only thing that differs between the two halves is who assembled the shelf, and what is measured is the price offered. Every shelf was wrapped (1), everyone had the same booklet (3) and no one chose a shelf (4), so those hypotheses name factors the design does not vary.

steps.stem: For many years, farmers in a certain valley believed that the valley's soil was too salty for earthworms to live in, so that earthworms could not be the cause of the narrow tunnels in their fields. A later study showed that this belief was wrong. Which of the following cannot be that study?
choices: Washing the salt out of a field in the valley with fresh water, and then checking whether earthworms are present in the field
Digging up soil from fields in the valley, and checking whether any earthworms are found in it
Preparing soil whose salt content is similar to that of the valley soil, and checking whether earthworms can live in it
Treating a field in the valley with a substance that kills only earthworms, and checking whether new tunnels stop appearing in it
explanation: Earthworms found after the salt has been washed out say nothing about whether they can live in the salty soil, which is what the belief is about. (2), (3) and (4) each test the soil as it actually is, so each could have shown the belief to be wrong.

steps.stem: A study found that when background music is played, people perform repetitive tasks better than they do in silence, whereas they perform tasks that require careful reading worse than they do in silence. Which of the following hypotheses does not explain this finding?
choices: Music raises a person's level of arousal, which prevents the drowsiness that repetitive work tends to cause; but careful reading requires a calm state of mind, and a raised level of arousal makes the reader restless and impairs their comprehension of the text

Music and reading draw on the same mental resources for processing language, so music interferes with reading; repetitive tasks make no use of these resources, and there the music relieves boredom and so helps the worker keep up their pace

Music diverts part of a person's attention away from the task at hand, and this harms performance; but the more demanding the task, the more attention it requires, so in a repetitive task, which requires little attention, the harm caused by the music becomes negligible
Music improves a person's mood, and a good mood helps performance of tasks that require little thought; but a good mood also makes people process information less carefully, which harms reading
explanation: A harm that becomes negligible cannot produce the improvement found in repetitive tasks. (1), (2) and (4) each give a reason for both halves of the finding.

steps.stem: An ecologist counted the nests of a certain seabird in two parts of an island: the cliffs on its northern coast and the sandy shore on its southern coast. She found that there are many more nests on the cliffs than on the shore, and that the difference between the two parts is not constant: a rise in the number of foxes on the island hardly affects the number of nests on the cliffs, but leads to a sharp drop in the number of nests on the shore. According to her findings, if there were more foxes on the island in 2023 than in 2022, it is reasonable that -
choices: the number of nests on the cliffs in 2023 was lower than in 2022
the number of nests on the shore in 2023 was higher than the number of nests on the cliffs in that year
in 2023 the number of nests on the shore was the same as in 2022, but on the cliffs it was much lower
the gap between the number of nests on the cliffs and the number on the shore was greater in 2023 than in 2022
explanation: More foxes leave the cliffs almost unchanged and cut the shore sharply, so the gap grows. (1) changes the part that foxes hardly affect, (3) swaps the roles of the two parts, and (2) contradicts the finding that the cliffs have far more nests, which is even truer after a rise in foxes.

steps.stem: A certain virus that attacks cucumber plants is carried from plant to plant by a small beetle. When the beetle feeds on the leaves of an infected plant, virus particles stick to its mouthparts, and it leaves them on the next plant it feeds on. If a single plant receives virus particles that come from several different infected plants, the particles can exchange genetic material inside that plant. This produces new forms of the virus, some of which are able to overcome the resistance that has been bred into modern cucumber varieties. Based on the paragraph, which of the following best explains why forms of the virus that can overcome this resistance arise sooner where the virus is common than where it is rare?
choices: In these areas, farmers grow older cucumber varieties that were never bred for resistance to the virus
In these areas, each beetle feeds on only one plant during its whole life
In these areas, a single plant is more likely to be fed on by beetles carrying particles from several different infected plants
In these areas, the beetle population is larger
explanation: New forms arise when particles from several infected plants meet inside one plant, and that is more likely where the virus is common. (4) is a step short (more beetles do not mean more sources per plant), (2) would stop the virus from moving between plants at all, and (1) brings in a fact from outside the paragraph that does not lead to resistance-breaking forms.

steps.title: Scientific reasoning — the words to know
steps.intro: Every study follows one chain: hypothesis → experiment → results → conclusion.

head: Term
What it means
rows: Cause and effect: if X changes, Y changes
X = the factor we change · Y = the result we measure
Groups identical except X — otherwise an alternative explanation
The comparison group: X absent, or X at a different level
The result — supports the hypothesis or contradicts it
Why the results came out as they did

tips: Two question types: understanding the study · understanding the findings.
Assumptions: flip it — if the opposite would ruin the experiment, it's an assumption.
Conclusions given: work out what must follow before reading the choices.
An explanation must cover every part of the finding.

steps.stem: The wings of certain insects, such as cicadas and dragonflies, stay free of bacteria, and not because they contain any substance that is poisonous to bacteria: their surface is covered with tiny spikes, packed so densely that they tear apart any bacterium that settles on them. The coatings used to protect hospital equipment from bacteria, by contrast, contain poisonous substances, and most of them lose their effect within a few months, as the substance wears away. Recently, engineers have succeeded in etching into a steel plate a pattern of tiny spikes whose density matches that of an insect's wing, and bacteria placed on the plate die although nothing poisonous has been added to it. Based on the paragraph, what new way of keeping surfaces free of bacteria over time might develop from the engineers' success?
choices: Extracting from insects the substances they produce against bacteria, and binding them to a surface that keeps them from wearing away
Arranging ordinary poisonous substances in tiny, densely packed spikes, so that they come into closer contact with bacteria and kill them faster
Covering existing coatings with a layer of steel thin enough to let the poison reach the bacteria while keeping the coating from wearing away
Shaping the surfaces of hospital equipment into patterns of tiny spikes that tear bacteria apart, so that the protection comes from the form of the surface and not from any poisonous substance
explanation: The discovery is protection without poison, and only (4) gives up the poisonous substance. (1) and (2) keep a poison and merely protect or arrange it, and (3) protects an existing coating instead of replacing it.

steps.stem: In a study, employees of a large company, some of whom walk to work and some of whom drive, were asked to name the streets along the route between their home and their office. The study yielded two findings. The first: the employees who walk named the streets along their route far more accurately than the employees who drive. The second: on their way to work, the employees who walk look at street signs much more often than the employees who drive. What is the relation between the two findings?
choices: The second finding can explain the first
The first finding is proof of the second
The two findings contradict each other
The second finding is a particular case of the first
explanation: Looking at street signs more often accounts for knowing the street names better, so the second finding explains the first. (2) reverses the direction, (3) sees a conflict where there is none, and (4) treats two different measures as a rule and an example of it.

steps.stem: A survey of the second-hand market in household goods found that a digital camera bought within the past two years is usually resold for only a little less than the current price of a new camera, whereas a dishwasher of the same age is usually resold for much less than the current price of a new dishwasher. Which of the following facts could explain this finding?
choices: Two years ago new dishwashers cost far more than new cameras, but the price of new dishwashers has fallen since then and is still falling
The price of new cameras has fallen noticeably over the past two years, while the price of new dishwashers has hardly changed
A new low-quality dishwasher generally costs more than a used high-quality one, whereas a new low-quality camera generally costs less than a used high-quality one
Cameras lose their quality with use faster than dishwashers do
explanation: If new cameras now cost less than they did, a camera bought two years ago is resold close to today's lower price, so the gap is small; stable dishwasher prices leave that gap wide. (1) has the wrong appliance getting cheaper, (3) compares quality levels rather than age, and (4) would widen the camera gap, not narrow it.

steps.stem: Prof. Levanon criticized a study for not examining what it set out to examine, and compared it to the following: "It is like wanting to know whether people who go on guided tours enjoy their trips, and checking for that purpose whether tour guides suffer from back pain more often than other people do." Which of the following studies is most likely to be the one Prof. Levanon criticized?
choices: A study that asked whether there is a connection between how much people believe they sleep and how much they actually sleep, by monitoring their sleep and questioning them
A study that asked whether the teaching of mathematics differs between schools in large cities and schools in small towns, by examining pupils from both
A study that asked whether people who read many novels are more understanding of others, by comparing how understanding novelists are with how understanding the general public is
A study that asked whether people who take a speed-reading course read faster, by comparing their reading speed before and after the course
explanation: The comparison faults a study for examining the people who provide something instead of the people who receive it: novelists stand to readers of novels as guides stand to tourists. (1), (2) and (4) each examine the very people the question is about.

steps.stem: A group of researchers found that a mouse kept in a cage with a running wheel does better on memory tasks than a mouse of the same strain kept in an identical cage without a wheel. They also found that the brain of the mouse with the wheel contains a higher level of a certain protein, which is present in the brains of mice of all strains. To find out whether it is this protein that improves the memory of the running mouse, the researchers repeated the experiment with new mice, making one change. Which of the following is most likely to be that change?
choices: They placed a substance known to improve memory in the cage of the mouse without the wheel
They used one mouse of the strain tested in the first experiment and one mouse of a different strain
They used two mice of the same strain, but of a strain other than the one tested in the first experiment
They used mice that had been genetically altered so that they cannot produce the protein
explanation: If mice that run but cannot produce the protein gain no memory advantage, the protein is the link. (1) changes the mouse without the wheel, and (2) and (3) change the strain, not the protein.

steps.stem: Researchers who examined skeletons of people who lived in a certain valley three thousand years ago found in the bones traces of a mineral that is present in the water of a nearby spring. The bones were remarkably strong and showed almost no signs of fractures, and the researchers concluded that the people of the valley drank from the spring and that its water strengthened their bones. Another researcher argued that the finding does not show that the spring water strengthened the bones, since the people of that period did hard physical work every day, which keeps bones strong in any case. Which of the following findings could weaken the other researcher's argument?
choices: Skeletons of people who lived in the region three thousand years ago, whose bones contain no traces of the mineral and show many more signs of fractures than the bones the researchers examined

Skeletons of people who lived at a later period, when most work was no longer physical, whose bones contain no traces of the mineral and show more signs of fractures than the bones the researchers examined
Remains of clay jars showing that the people of the valley at that time drew large amounts of water from the spring
Skeletons of people who lived at a time when other means of strengthening the bones were known, whose bones contain traces of the mineral
explanation: People of the same period did the same hard work, yet without the mineral their bones broke far more, so the work cannot be the whole explanation. (2) is exactly what the critic would expect, and (3) and (4) do not bear on the argument about work.

steps.stem: A certain kind of spider spins its webs among the branches of a certain shrub. A study found that shrubs with spider webs on them lost fewer leaves to caterpillars than shrubs without webs. The authors of the study hypothesized that the spiders catch the moths that come to lay eggs on the shrub, so that fewer caterpillars hatch on it. Another researcher hypothesized instead that the spiders choose, in the first place, to spin their webs on shrubs that are less exposed to caterpillars, since such shrubs offer them steadier shelter. The authors carried out a further test whose results allowed them to confirm one of the two hypotheses. Which of the following tests is most likely to be the one they carried out?
choices: They covered a number of shrubs with nets that keep moths out and measured the leaf loss of those shrubs
They moved spiders onto randomly chosen shrubs and measured the leaf loss of those shrubs
They measured the leaf loss of shrubs that held webs of other kinds of spider
They counted the moths caught by each spider, and not only the leaves lost by the shrubs
explanation: Random placement removes the spiders' choice; if the shrubs they were placed on still lose fewer leaves, the spiders themselves are the cause. (1), (3) and (4) cannot tell the spiders' effect apart from their choice of shrub.

steps.stem: A certain fungus is found in the soil of almost every orchard in a certain region, yet only about one tree in ten in these orchards develops root rot. Which of the following claims, if true, explains these facts?
choices: The spread of the fungus in the soil is what causes root rot
The fungus usually appears in the soil after a certain bacterium has appeared there, and it is the bacterium that sometimes causes root rot
The presence of the fungus leads to the appearance of a certain bacterium, and the two together always cause root rot
The fungus is only one of the factors that lead to root rot, but root rot cannot develop where the fungus is absent
explanation: A condition that is necessary but not sufficient fits a fungus that is almost everywhere and a disease that is not. (1) and (3) would make root rot common wherever the fungus is found, and (2) leaves the fungus with no part in the facts at all.

steps.stem: Can horses tell from where a person is looking which object the person is paying attention to? A new study suggests that they can. The researcher placed three covered bowls, each containing food, in front of the horses, and on each trial looked steadily at a different bowl; the horses tended to approach the bowl the researcher was looking at. The researcher argued that the horses had this ability before the experiment began and did not acquire it during the experiment, and cited a finding from the experiment in support. Which of the following findings is most likely to be the one cited?
choices: Young horses approached the bowl that the researcher looked at more often than old horses did
In the first trials the horses approached each of the three bowls equally often
The rate at which the horses approached the bowl that the researcher looked at was no lower in the first trials of the experiment than in its last trials
Not all of the horses that took part in the experiment approached the bowl that the researcher looked at equally often
explanation: Learning during the experiment would show as improvement from trial to trial, so a rate that is as high at the start as at the end points to an ability the horses already had. (2) suggests the opposite, and (1) and (4) compare horses with one another rather than early trials with late ones.

steps.stem: A study of river valleys that had flooded found that in the first years after a flood the trees along the river grow quickly, and that their growth then slows. Dr. Amsalem argued that the cause is the layer of silt that the flood leaves on the ground. Which of the following findings does not strengthen Dr. Amsalem's claim?
choices: Silt contains nitrogen compounds that the trees need for growth and that are scarce in the soil of the valleys
Silt speeds the growth of the grasses that compete with the trees for water
Researchers who planted tree seedlings in soils mixed with silt found that the fresher the silt, the faster the seedlings grew
In valleys where the silt was washed away by rain soon after the flood, no rapid growth of trees was observed
explanation: Helping the trees' competitors would slow the trees, not speed them. (1) supplies a mechanism, (3) explains why the effect fades as the silt ages, and (4) shows that without the silt there is no effect.

steps.stem: Root-knot nematodes are tiny worms that live inside the roots of tomato plants, where pesticides hardly reach them. Nevertheless, many growers reduce their numbers by growing marigolds in a field for a season before planting tomatoes there. Which of the following data could explain why growing marigolds is effective against root-knot nematodes?
choices: Marigold roots release into the soil a substance near which the worms cannot survive
Marigold roots react with pesticides in the soil and lower their concentration without reducing their effectiveness
Marigolds give off a smell that drives away the beetles that feed on root-knot nematodes
Marigold seeds cost far less than most of the pesticides on the market
explanation: Only (1) links the marigolds to the death of the worms. (3) would actually help the worms, and (2) and (4) concern pesticides and cost.

steps.stem: A researcher asked experienced chess players to look briefly at chessboards and then set up the positions from memory. Some of the boards showed positions taken from real games, and others showed pieces placed at random. The players reproduced the positions from real games much more accurately. The researcher attributed this mainly to the players' familiarity with the kind of positions that arise in real games, but she also raised a second possibility: that the random boards held more pieces than the boards from real games, and were therefore harder to take in. She then carried out a second experiment, whose result showed that the second factor is of minor importance. Which of the following is most likely to be the result of the second experiment?
choices: Beginners, who had played few games, reproduced random positions as accurately as positions taken from real games
Experienced players reproduced positions from games they had played themselves more accurately than positions from games played by others
Experienced players reproduced positions from real games that held many pieces more accurately than random positions that held few pieces
Players who were asked to count the pieces on a board did so faster and more accurately when the board held few pieces
explanation: Only (3) sets the two factors against each other: familiar boards that are hard to take in still beat unfamiliar boards that are easy, so the number of pieces matters less. (2) shows that familiarity has an effect but says nothing about the number of pieces, (1) concerns players with no familiarity at all, and (4) is about the number of pieces alone.

steps.stem: At a certain bank, most of the loan applications submitted by small businesses were approved, whereas only a minority of the applications submitted by large businesses were approved. An examination of each branch, however, found that in every branch the proportion of approved applications among those submitted by small businesses equaled the proportion among those submitted by large businesses. Which of the following facts could explain these data?
choices: Most of the small businesses applied at branches where loans are rarely approved, and most of the large businesses at branches where loans are approved easily
Every branch received the same number of applications from small businesses as from large businesses
Most of the small businesses and most of the large businesses applied at the same branches
Most of the small businesses applied at branches where loans are approved easily, and most of the large businesses at branches where loans are rarely approved
explanation: Equal rates in every branch but unequal rates overall mean that the two groups applied at different kinds of branches, and the group with the higher overall rate must have gone mainly to the lenient ones. (1) has the direction reversed, and (2) and (3) would make the overall rates equal.

steps.stem: A certain kind of clay has an unusual property: left undisturbed, it is firm, but a strong shake turns it at once into a liquid. Its tiny, flat particles have edges whose electric charge is opposite to that of their faces, so each particle's edge clings to another's face, and the particles form a loose framework, like a house of cards, with water in its spaces. A strong shake breaks these contacts; the particles fall flat, slide over one another in the water, and the clay flows. When the shaking stops, they slowly cling together again and the clay becomes firm. In most other clays this does not happen. Which of the following explanations about the particles of those clays best fits the paragraph?
choices: Their edges and faces do not carry opposite electric charges
They are larger than the particles of this clay
A strong shake does not make them flow
When the shaking stops, they cling to one another again
explanation: The paragraph names the opposite charges of edges and faces as what builds the framework, so their absence explains why nothing happens. (3) restates the difference instead of explaining it, (4) is true of this clay as well, and (2) brings in a property the paragraph never links to the effect.

steps.stem: In 2015 a certain city changed the color of the lines marking its bicycle lanes from white to bright red. The change was expected to make the roads safer for cyclists, since red lines stand out to drivers more than white ones. And indeed, in the first months after the change the number of accidents involving cyclists in the city fell sharply. But the fall did not last, and two years later the number of such accidents had returned to its former level. Which of the following best explains why the fall in the number of accidents did not last?
choices: In 2015 the city began repainting its remaining white lanes red, and by 2017 no white lanes were left
In the first months after the change, drivers paid special attention to the bicycle lanes because the new markings were unfamiliar to them
Red lines are easier for drivers to notice than white lines, especially at night
In 2015 the speed limit on the city's main roads was raised by ten kilometers an hour
explanation: Attention that fades as the markings become familiar explains a fall that is later reversed. (1) and (3) would predict a lasting fall, and (4) took effect just when accidents fell, so it cannot explain why they later rose.

steps.stem: Liora claimed that she could tell exactly how many coins are in a jar just by shaking it. To prove it, she shook a jar of coins and announced that it held 214 coins. Gil did not believe her and wanted to test her claim; but counting all the coins would take a long time, so he thought of a much quicker test. Which of the following is most likely to be the test Gil thought of?
choices: Gil will pour the coins into two smaller jars; Liora will shake each of them and say how many coins it holds, and Gil will check whether the two numbers add up to 214
Gil's brother will also shake the jar and say how many coins he thinks it holds, and Gil will compare his number with Liora's
Liora will shake a second jar and say how many coins it holds; Gil will count the coins in that jar and compare

Gil will take a few coins out of the jar without telling Liora how many; Liora will shake the jar again and say how many coins are left, and Gil will check whether the difference equals the number he took out
explanation: Only a real ability could follow a change whose size Gil alone knows. Anyone can make the two numbers in (1) add up to 214, (2) compares two guesses, and (3) requires the full count Gil wanted to avoid.

steps.stem: A study of how lighting affects people at work yielded two findings: people who worked on a problem in a dimly lit room came up with more original solutions than people who worked on the same problem in a brightly lit room; and people who checked documents for errors in a brightly lit room found more errors than people who checked the same documents in a dimly lit room. On the basis of these findings, the researchers made a number of recommendations. Which of the following is least likely to be one of them?
choices: Proofreaders who check texts for errors should do their work in brightly lit rooms
The lighting of a workroom should be chosen according to the kind of work that is done in it
The less original a person's thinking, the more important it is for them to work in a brightly lit room
Advertising teams that meet in order to think of new ideas for campaigns should meet in a dimly lit room
explanation: Dim light is what helps original thinking, yet (3) sends the person who most needs that help into bright light. (1), (2) and (4) follow directly from the findings.

steps.stem: In an experiment, researchers gave each participant a notebook with a red cover. After a while, each participant was offered the chance to exchange it for a notebook with a blue cover that had been given to another participant. Most of the participants refused. The researchers hypothesized that the refusals stemmed from a preference for the color red, but a follow-up experiment showed that this hypothesis was wrong. Which of the following best describes the follow-up experiment?
choices: Each participant received a notebook with a blue cover and was later offered an identical notebook with a red cover in exchange; most refused
Each participant received a notebook with a red cover and was later offered a thinner notebook with a blue cover in exchange; most refused
Each participant received a notebook with a green cover and was later offered a thicker notebook with a red cover in exchange; most agreed
Each participant received a notebook with a red cover and was later offered a thicker notebook with a red cover in exchange; most agreed
explanation: People who refuse to give up a blue notebook for an identical red one cannot be driven by a preference for red. (2) and (3) fit a preference for red, and (4) does not test color at all.

steps.stem: In an experiment, participants were shown ten paintings and asked which one they liked best. Each participant then received false information about the choices of the others: some were told that most of the participants had chosen the same painting as they had, and others that almost no one had. Finally, the participants answered questions designed to reveal their mood. Which of the following is most likely to have been the purpose of the experiment?
choices: To examine how mood affects the tendency to choose paintings that others like
To examine whether, in an experiment, people try to choose paintings that others like
To examine whether people prefer to feel different from others or to feel similar to them
To examine how choosing between paintings affects mood
explanation: The only thing varied is what the participants hear about how similar their choice is to others', and the only thing measured afterward is mood. (1) reverses cause and effect, and (2) and (4) name factors the design does not isolate.

steps.stem: A food critic wrote: "Something strange is happening in our city: every year more mediocre restaurants open here than ever before, yet nearly all the restaurant reviews published in the local press are favorable." Which of the following data could explain the situation the critic describes?
choices: Food critics often disagree about what makes a restaurant good
Most food critics believe that mediocre restaurants should be reviewed harshly, so as to warn diners
Food critics prefer not to write about restaurants that disappointed them
More restaurant reviews are published in the local press today than in the past
explanation: If critics write only about the restaurants they liked, the reviews will be favorable however many mediocre restaurants open. (2) predicts the opposite, and (1) and (4) do not explain why the reviews lean toward praise.

steps.stem: In an experiment, two groups of participants read the same short story and rated it according to several literary criteria. Group A read the story in an uncomfortably cold room; group B read it in a room at a normal temperature. After giving their ratings, the members of group A were asked whether the cold had affected their judgment, and if so, how. Most of them said that the cold had affected them strongly and had led them to rate the story lower than they would have otherwise; in fact, however, the ratings given by group A were higher than those given by group B. Which of the following is most likely to have been the purpose of the experiment?
choices: To examine whether people consider their own judgment better than that of others
To examine whether reading in the cold leads to harsher judgment than reading at a normal temperature
To examine whether lack of concentration causes people to rate a story higher
To examine whether people judge correctly how uncomfortable conditions affect their judgment
explanation: The experiment sets what the participants said the cold did to their ratings against what it actually did. (2) covers only the comparison between the two groups, and (1) and (3) are not tested at all.

steps.stem: At a telephone sales center, the team in one of the rooms has two supervisors: one supervises the morning shift and the other the evening shift. Recently the center's manager told the morning supervisor that he intends to replace her, since the team sells less during her shift than during the evening shift. The supervisor argued that the low sales are not her fault, and proposed a check to the manager. Which of the following is most likely to be the check she proposed?
choices: To check whether the prices of the products the center sells have recently gone up
To check whether in the center's other rooms, too, more is sold in the evening shift than in the morning shift
To check whether the center has recently run short of products that customers often ask for
To check whether in the center's other rooms, too, there are supervisors who work only in the morning shift or only in the evening shift
explanation: If every room sells more in the evening, the shift explains the gap, not the supervisor. (1) and (3) would affect both shifts alike, and (4) is about staffing, not sales.

steps.stem: A study found that people who regularly do crossword puzzles have, on average, a larger vocabulary than people who rarely do them. The researchers concluded that doing crossword puzzles enlarges a person's vocabulary. Which of the following could serve as an alternative explanation of the study's findings?
choices: People with a large vocabulary enjoy crossword puzzles more, since they manage to solve them
The ability to acquire a large vocabulary is innate, whereas a liking for crossword puzzles is not
People who solve puzzles of any kind have, on average, a larger vocabulary
Doing crossword puzzles strengthens the regions of the brain responsible for language
explanation: The large vocabulary may lead to the puzzles rather than the reverse. (4) is the researchers' own explanation, and (2) and (3) do not explain the link between these puzzles and vocabulary.

steps.stem: A doctor wished to examine whether the rise in the number of people who come to the emergency room with back injuries in winter is caused by shoveling snow. She gathered a sample of people who came to the emergency room with back injuries in winter and checked how many of them had shoveled snow shortly before. To make her results unambiguous, she must compare them with the result of a further check. Which of the following checks is best suited for this?
choices: Among people who came in with back injuries in winter, what proportion shoveled snow only after coming in
Among people who had not shoveled snow at that time, what proportion came in with back injuries in winter
Among people who had shoveled snow at that time, what proportion did not come in with back injuries in winter
Among people who came in with back injuries in winter, what proportion had shoveled snow
explanation: The rate among people who did not shovel snow is the baseline that the rate among those who did must exceed. (4) repeats the doctor's own check, and (1) and (3) provide no group to compare with.

steps.stem: Dana argues that teachers, sometimes without noticing, give more encouragement to pupils whose parents are university graduates, and that this is one of the reasons these pupils do better at school. Yoav, by contrast, argues that teachers merely respond to differences in the pupils' own eagerness to learn, which stem from the pupils' homes. Which of the following studies could help decide between the two claims?
choices: Observing pupils and checking to what extent their achievements match their parents' level of education
Following the books that parents with different levels of education buy for their children
Interviewing pupils and asking them whether they feel their teachers treat them differently from their classmates
Giving teachers the same essay, telling some of them that the pupil's parents are university graduates and others that they are not, and comparing the comments the two groups write
explanation: With the same essay in every teacher's hands, any difference in the comments comes from the label and not from the pupil's eagerness. (1), (2) and (3) cannot separate the two explanations.

steps.stem: Researchers presented two groups of participants with a story about a driver who backed into a parked car, causing damage of 4,000 shekels, and drove away without leaving a note. Group A was told that the driver had not noticed hitting the car; group B was told that the driver had noticed and decided to leave. The researchers hypothesized that the guiltier a person is thought to be, the more people tend to remember the details of the case in a way that makes the act more serious. Which of the following findings supports the researchers' hypothesis?
choices: Asked to state the cost of the damage, group A gave on average a sum of about 4,000 shekels, and group B a sum well above 4,000 shekels
Asked the name of the street where the accident took place, more members of group A than of group B remembered it
Asked their opinion of the cost of the damage, most of group A thought 4,000 shekels an exaggerated sum, and most of group B thought it a fair one
Asked whether the story mentioned that the driver was rushing to a hospital, more members of group B than of group A answered yes
explanation: The driver seen as guiltier is remembered as having caused more damage. (4) would make the act less serious, and (2) and (3) do not show memory that adds to the severity of the act.

steps.stem: The human-resources manager of a large company found that employees who took the company's optional workshop on time management were promoted, on average, sooner than employees who did not take it, and she concluded that the workshop helped the employees who took it. Her colleague Amos holds that there is another explanation: the more ambitious employees are the ones who chose to take the workshop, and since they are ambitious they were promoted sooner. Which of the following conclusions could be undermined by an alternative explanation of the kind Amos proposed?
choices: Datum: patients who received a new ointment, given by lottery to half the patients at a clinic, recovered faster, on average, than patients who did not. Conclusion: the ointment is effective
Datum: children who take part in an optional after-school chess club get higher marks in mathematics, on average, than children who do not. Conclusion: playing chess improves mathematical ability
Datum: people who sleep more are, on average, less irritable than people who sleep less. Conclusion: a person who sleeps more than another person is probably also less irritable
Datum: a survey among the passengers of the "Nof" bus company found that it is the most punctual company in the country. Conclusion: no bus company is more punctual than "Nof"
explanation: Children who choose a chess club may be the ones who are strong in mathematics to begin with, the same self-selection Amos points to. In (1) the ointment was given by lottery, (3) draws no causal conclusion, and (4) has a different flaw.
